nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive when describing character or experience, and neutral to negative when describing damage.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'weathered' for wood, stone, boats, barns and faces to suggest age and years outdoors, such as 'a weathered face' or 'weathered hands'. Calling a person 'weathered' can be a respectful way to suggest they have hard, practical experience. It is more literary than everyday speech.

distinctions.note: Worn describes general wear from use, while weathered specifically describes changes caused by exposure to the elements.
Experienced describes skill or knowledge gained over time, while weathered can describe physical signs of exposure as well as a seasoned character.

examples.everyday: My grandpa has a weathered face from fifty years of fishing.
examples.professional: The weathered bridge deck needs resurfacing before winter.
examples.analytical: The poem's imagery of stone and salt suggests that time wears down human pride more surely than any single defeat.

nuance.analogy: A weathered boot is one that has been rained on and dried in the sun for years, and now shows its history.
nuance.etymology: From the verb weather (to expose to the weather), plus the past participle ending -ed.
common_mistakes: Using 'weathered' for objects damaged by people, where 'worn' or 'damaged' is more natural.
Pronouncing the -ed as a separate syllable, as in WETH-er-ed.

senses.definition: What someone plans to do on the weekend; a common small-talk topic.
senses.example: Before the meeting, everyone chatted about weekend plans while the coffee brewed.

core.definition: What you intend to do on Saturday and Sunday; a very common topic of casual conversation, especially on Friday or Monday.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable of weekend, WEEK, not the second. The final d is light, so the phrase flows as WEEK-end-PLANS.

nuance.connotation: Positive
nuance.usage_note: Americans ask What are you doing this weekend? or Any weekend plans? on Friday or Monday. A natural reply is Nothing much, just relaxing, or We're going to my sister's. Keep the answer short; it is friendly small talk, not an invitation.

distinctions.note: Plans is general and can cover any activity at home or away, while a trip means traveling somewhere.
A schedule is a fixed timetable, while weekend plans are informal and often flexible.

examples.everyday: Any weekend plans? I'm hoping to finally finish painting the fence.
examples.professional: I'm on call this weekend, so my weekend plans are pretty flexible if the team needs me.
examples.analytical: Weekend plans reveal what people value when no obligation constrains them, which makes them a useful lens for studying leisure.

nuance.analogy: Weekend plans are like a blank page that people fill in on Friday afternoon.
nuance.etymology: Weekend combines week and end; plans comes through French from Latin planus, flat.
common_mistakes: Saying plans in the weekend; Americans say on the weekend or for the weekend.
Pronouncing weekend as wee-kend with equal stress on both syllables.

conversation.text: "Any weekend plans?" "Just relaxing. Maybe a hike on Sunday."
What are your weekend plans? Anything fun?
The rain totally ruined our weekend plans.

senses.definition: Synonym of well-fed.
senses.example: The pediatrician said the toddler was healthy and well-nourished at her checkup.

core.definition: Receiving enough food of the right kinds, so that the body is healthy and developing normally.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on NUR, with the r strongly pronounced, and the ou in 'nourish' is silent. Say it as two syllables, 'NUR-isht,' not 'nour-ISH-ed.'

nuance.connotation: Positive and neutral; it describes health and adequate diet, often in medical or public health contexts.
nuance.usage_note: Doctors, nurses, and public health workers use this term often, and Americans use it in conversation about children, pets, or patients. In everyday talk, 'well-fed' is more common, but it sounds like someone simply eats a lot. Use 'well-nourished' when you mean good nutrition.

distinctions.note: 'Well-fed' refers to having eaten enough; 'well-nourished' refers to getting the right nutrients over time, which is more precise.
'Healthy' is a broad term for overall good condition; 'well-nourished' names one specific cause of good health.

examples.everyday: Our dog looks great, and the vet said he's well-nourished, so I'll keep the same food.
examples.professional: Our nutrition program tracks whether children in each school district are well-nourished throughout the school year.
examples.analytical: Studies of public health measure whether a population is well-nourished, not merely whether it has access to enough calories.

nuance.analogy: Like a garden that gets both water and the right fertilizer, not just a lot of water: growth depends on the right nutrients.
nuance.etymology: From Old French norrir and Latin nutrire 'to feed, suckle,' combined with well from Old English wel.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the ou as in 'our'; the ou is silent, so the word sounds like 'NUR-isht.'
Using it as a synonym for 'overweight' or 'heavy'; it describes healthy nutrition, not body size.

senses.definition: Admired, highly thought of, approved of.
senses.example: She is a well-regarded pastor whose sermons on grace draw visitors from across the county.

core.definition: Admired and respected by others, usually for skill, quality, or good character.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on GARD, which is a broad 'ahr' sound in American speech. The middle syllable 'ri' is reduced, so say it quickly as 'rih.'

nuance.connotation: Positive; it signals reputation and trust, often used for schools, professionals, and brands.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this for doctors, universities, restaurants, and writers when their reputation is strong. It sounds natural in reviews, recommendations, and job talk. Saying 'a well-regarded doctor' is more polite than 'a famous doctor,' which can sound like celebrity.

distinctions.note: 'Respected' focuses on how people feel about the person's character or judgment; 'well-regarded' often refers to a reputation for quality or skill.
'Popular' means many people like someone or something; 'well-regarded' means experts or serious judges think highly of it.

examples.everyday: My dentist is well-regarded in town, so I booked an appointment with her right away.
examples.professional: Our well-regarded engineering team has delivered three major releases on schedule this year.
examples.analytical: A well-regarded theologian can still be wrong, so the authority of his reputation must be tested against the text.

nuance.analogy: Like a restaurant with a long line of loyal customers who keep recommending it to friends.
nuance.etymology: From re- and Old French garder 'to watch, guard,' via Old French regarder 'to look at.'
common_mistakes: Using 'well-regarded' for something that is simply popular; it implies serious respect, not just attention.
Saying 'regarded well' in place of the hyphenated adjective before a noun.

senses.definition: The act of making something wet.
The act of accidental urination on or in something.
senses.example: The toddler had a wetting accident on the carpet during naptime.

senses.definition: An act of murdering or seriously injuring someone.
senses.example: The gangster's ominous threat promised a wetting for anyone who talked to the police.

senses.definition: That makes (something) wet.
senses.example: The wetting rain soaked the picnic blankets before we could pack up.

core.definition: The act of making something wet, such as wetting a cloth before you clean a window.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable. The t between vowels is a quick flap that sounds like a light d, and the ng ends the word without an extra g sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in the basic sense. It becomes embarrassing or negative when it refers to accidental urination, especially by children.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use wetting as a noun mostly in cooking, cleaning, or science, as in wetting the sponge or wetting agent. The sense of accidental urination is discussed in medical or parenting contexts, where bedwetting is the usual term. The sense of murder or serious injury is rare and dated, so avoid it.

distinctions.note: Wetting is the act or process of making something wet, while wetness is the state of being wet.
Soaking means leaving something in liquid for a long time, while wetting can be brief and light.
Bedwetting is the specific everyday and medical term for urinating in bed at night, while wetting alone is general.

examples.everyday: Give the sponge a quick wetting before you wipe down the counter.
examples.professional: The wetting agent in this formula should reduce the surface tension on the metal.
examples.analytical: Wetting is best understood as the balance of adhesive and cohesive forces at the boundary between a solid and a liquid.

nuance.analogy: Like a sponge that must take in water before it can spread it evenly.
nuance.etymology: From wet (Old English wǣt) plus the suffix -ing.
common_mistakes: Using wetting for the general condition of being wet; say wetness for that.
Using the rare murder sense in modern speech, which sounds odd or archaic.

senses.definition: An informal greeting.
senses.example: Hey Jake, what's going on? Long time no see!

senses.definition: An expression of concern, asking for an explanation.
senses.example: What's going on? Why are you crying in the parking lot?

core.definition: An informal greeting meaning 'How are you?' or 'What's new?', used to open a casual conversation.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on ON, the last word, and 'going' is reduced to 'goh-ing.' In American speech 'what's' often sounds like 'wuts,' with the final s clearly audible.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and friendly as a greeting; it can sound concerned or pointed when used as a real question.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this constantly as an opener with coworkers, neighbors, and friends, usually without expecting a detailed answer. A natural reply is 'Not much, how about you?' or 'Same old, same old.' If something is actually wrong, the same words can become a real question, so listen to tone and context.

distinctions.note: The two are nearly identical as greetings, but 'what's going on?' is slightly more common in conversation across the US.
'What's up?' is shorter and more casual, while 'what's going on?' sounds slightly more inquiring.

collocations: what's going on with the project?

examples.everyday: Hey Marcus, what's going on? Long time no see.
examples.professional: Morning, Dana, what's going on? Did you get a chance to look at the draft?
examples.analytical: Sociolinguists note that 'what's going on?' often works as a greeting that expects only a brief reply, not a true report of events.

nuance.analogy: Like a porch wave: it signals that you see the other person, and the reply is usually just a small nod.
common_mistakes: Answering with a long account of your day; the greeting expects a short reply.
Confusing the greeting use with the concern sense, which is used when something is actually wrong.

senses.definition: Asking about the ingredients of a dish.

core.definition: A question asking what ingredients a dish or food contains, often because you want to know if it has something you avoid.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on WHAT'S, and 'in' and 'this' are light and quick. Say 'wuts' with a short vowel, and don't pronounce a strong 'th' on 'this' in fast speech.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a polite, ordinary question and carries no suspicion when asked at a restaurant.
nuance.usage_note: Americans ask this at restaurants, potlucks, or when a friend serves a home-cooked meal, often when they have an allergy or dietary restriction. A natural reply is a list, such as 'Mostly chicken, garlic, and a little cream.' You can make it more specific with 'Is there any nuts in this?' but the correct form is 'Are there any nuts in this?'.

distinctions.note: 'What's in this?' points at a specific dish or item in front of you, while 'What's in it?' is used when the item is already named or understood.
'What's this made of?' is more general and often asks about materials for objects, while for food, 'What's in this?' is the natural choice.

examples.everyday: This soup is so good, what's in this? I can taste something smoky.
examples.professional: Before we order for the team lunch, can you check what's in this vendor's sandwich so we can flag the allergens?
examples.analytical: When a food label omits ingredients, the consumer's question 'What's in this?' becomes a demand for transparency about what the product actually contains.

nuance.analogy: Like asking a chef for the recipe card, it opens up the full list behind the finished plate.
common_mistakes: Saying 'What is in this?' in casual speech is correct but sounds stiff; Americans usually contract it to 'What's in this?'.
Using 'What's include this?' instead of 'What's in this?'; 'include' is a verb and cannot follow 'What's' here.

conversation.text: This is amazing. What's in this?
What's in this? I have a nut allergy.
Wow, what's in this sauce? It's so good.

senses.definition: Asking the caller's name.

core.definition: A polite way to ask a caller for their name before connecting them or taking a message.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on KAW in 'calling' and on PLEEZ in 'please', with the first word reduced to 'hooz'. The final 'please' is often reduced to 'pleez' in quick speech.

nuance.connotation: Polite and professional. It shows courtesy and is standard in offices and customer service.
nuance.usage_note: Receptionists, assistants, and customer service staff say this constantly in American workplaces. At home it can sound stiff unless you are being deliberately formal. A natural reply gives your name and affiliation, such as 'It's Dana Lee from Harbor Bank.'

distinctions.note: Who's calling is casual and common, while adding please makes it more polite and suitable for work.
May I ask who's calling is more formal still and is often used with unknown or senior callers.

collocations: Who's calling, please, and what is this regarding?
Can I ask who's calling, please?
Thank you for holding. Who's calling, please?

examples.everyday: Hi, who's calling, please? My husband is in the shower right now.
examples.professional: Thank you for holding. Who's calling, please, so I can connect you to the right department?
examples.analytical: The receptionist asks who's calling, please because the caller's identity determines which department should take the call.

nuance.analogy: The question is like a doorman asking for your name before letting you into a building.
nuance.etymology: From who's, a contraction of who is, plus the verb call from Old English ceallian, with please from Old French plaisir.
common_mistakes: Dropping 'please' in a business setting, which can sound abrupt.
Pronouncing 'calling' with a short 'a' as in 'cabbing'.
Responding with 'me' or 'I'm the one who called' instead of giving your name.

conversation.text: "Is Mr. Green available?" "Who's calling, please?"
Who's calling, please? I'll let her know.
"Who's calling, please?" "It's Tom Reyes from the bank."

senses.definition: A person or company that buys merchandise from manufacturers, importers, or distributors and resells the merchandise to retail businesses and to business and institutional end users.
senses.example: The wholesaler sold cases of canned tomatoes to dozens of local restaurants.

core.definition: A business that buys large amounts of goods from producers and sells them in bulk to retailers or other businesses.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress is on WHOLE, with a secondary stress on SALE. The final -er is a rhotic American 'ur' sound, so pronounce the r clearly rather than saying 'wholesaler' as 'wholesale-uh'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes a business role in the supply chain without judgment, though it can imply a middleman who adds cost or distance.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use wholesaler in business, shopping, economics, and logistics discussions, such as 'We buy our paper from a wholesaler.' It is more formal than everyday shopping talk, where people usually say 'the supplier' or 'the distributor.' Wholesalers often sell only to businesses, so ordinary customers generally buy from retailers unless they have a business license.

distinctions.note: A retailer sells directly to individual consumers, while a wholesaler sells in bulk to retailers and other businesses.
A distributor often handles delivery and may represent a manufacturer's products in a region, while a wholesaler buys and resells goods on its own account.

examples.everyday: My cousin runs a small bakery, and she buys flour in big sacks from a wholesaler.
examples.professional: We're switching to a regional wholesaler to cut our distribution costs before the holiday season.
examples.analytical: The wholesaler occupies a middle position in the supply chain, absorbing the risk of inventory between the manufacturer and the retailer.

nuance.analogy: Like a warehouse that buys entire pallets from factories and sells them in cases to corner shops.
nuance.etymology: From wholesale (from whole and sale, meaning sale in bulk) with the agent suffix -er.
common_mistakes: Confusing wholesaler with retailer, which sells to individual customers.
Pronouncing the final -er as a weak 'uh' without the American r sound.
Using wholesale as a noun for a person; the person is a wholesaler.

senses.definition: The state or condition of being willful; stubbornness.
senses.example: His willfulness kept him from accepting help, even when he clearly needed it.

core.definition: Stubborn insistence on doing what one wants, even after being warned, advised or asked to stop.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on WIL. The middle syllable -ful is reduced to 'fuhl', not 'full', and the ending is a weak 'nus'. American spelling uses one l in 'willful'.

nuance.connotation: Negative, suggesting stubbornness and disregard for others' advice or rules.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use willfulness to describe a person, often a child or a stubborn adult, who refuses to listen. In legal and business writing, willful is also used to mean deliberate, as in 'willful violation' of a rule. In casual talk, people more often say 'stubborn' or 'headstrong'.

distinctions.note: Stubbornness is the everyday word for refusing to change one's mind, while willfulness adds the idea of deliberately acting against advice or rules.
Obstinacy is more formal and literary, emphasizing a fixed refusal to yield, while willfulness can also describe deliberate actions.
Determination is positive and suggests focused effort toward a goal, while willfulness suggests refusing reasonable guidance.

examples.everyday: Her willfulness drives me crazy when she refuses to wear a coat, even when it's freezing outside.
examples.professional: The team's willfulness in skipping code review caused the outage, even after two warnings from the lead.
examples.analytical: Many moral philosophers distinguish mere willfulness, acting on whatever one happens to desire, from a self-governed will that acts on reasons.

nuance.analogy: Willfulness is like a car with the steering stuck: it keeps going its own way no matter how the driver turns the wheel.
nuance.etymology: From will, plus the adjective suffix -ful and the noun suffix -ness.
common_mistakes: Spelling it 'wilfulness' with the British double-l-less form in American writing; use 'willfulness' in the US.
Confusing willfulness with willingness, which is positive and means readiness to help or agree.

senses.definition: To subject (granular material, especially food grain) to a current of air separating heavier and lighter components, as grain from chaff.
senses.example: Farmers winnow the harvested wheat to separate the grain from the chaff.

senses.definition: To separate, sift, analyze, or test by separating items having different values.
senses.example: They winnowed the field to twelve.

senses.definition: To blow upon or toss about by blowing; to set in motion as with a fan or wings.
senses.example: The breeze winnowed the dry leaves across the porch and scattered them over the lawn.

senses.definition: (dated) To move about with a flapping motion, as of wings; to flutter.
senses.example: The hawk winnowed its wings above the canyon before diving toward the river.
senses.label: dated

senses.definition: That which winnows or which is used in winnowing; a contrivance for fanning or winnowing grain.
senses.example: The old farmhand kept a hand winnow in the barn for cleaning the oats.

senses.definition: The act of winnowing.
senses.example: The winnow of the rice took all morning under the hot August sun.

core.definition: To separate the valuable parts from the less valuable, usually by sifting or testing out the weaker items.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, WIN, and the second syllable is a clear 'oh.' The 'w' is pronounced and the final sound is a long 'o,' not 'ow.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive. It suggests careful, thoughtful selection that removes what is not useful.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'winnow' in formal writing, academic work, and professional decision-making, for example 'winnow the candidates down to five.' It is less common in casual speech, where people say 'narrow down' or 'cut down.' The literal sense of blowing chaff from grain is used in farming and history.

distinctions.note: Sift is more physical or everyday and can apply to flour or sand; winnow is more formal and focuses on removing less valuable items.
Narrow down is common and casual; winnow sounds more formal and suggests a careful process of removal.

examples.everyday: We need to winnow the restaurant list down to two places before we decide where to eat.
examples.professional: The hiring committee will winnow the applicant pool to six finalists before the first round of interviews.
examples.analytical: The author winnows the historical sources, separating reliable testimony from later legend, which strengthens the argument's evidence.

nuance.analogy: To winnow is like tossing grain in the wind so the heavy kernels fall back and the chaff blows away.
nuance.etymology: From Old English windwian, from wind (moving air).
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it 'wye-noh' as if the first vowel were a long i.
Misspelling it as 'winow' with one n, which is incorrect.

winnow.etymology: From Middle English *wyndwen*, from Old English *windwian* (“to winnow, fan, ventilate”), from **windwōn*, from Proto-Germanic **windwōną*, **winþijaną* (“to throw about, winnow”), from Proto-Indo-European **wē-* (“to winnow, thresh”).

senses.definition: The art of a wizard; sorcery.
Something, such as an advanced technology, that gives the appearance of magic.
senses.example: The engineers' wizardry with machine learning made the old database feel almost magical.

senses.definition: Great ability in some specified field.
senses.example: He used his computing wizardry to automate the search-and-replace process.

core.definition: Magic performed by a wizard, or an extraordinary skill that seems almost magical.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, WIZ. The middle syllable is a reduced schwa, and the final syllable is 'dree', with the r pronounced clearly.

nuance.connotation: Positive in most uses. It praises skill that seems almost magical; in fantasy or literary contexts it can be neutral or ominous.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use wizardry most often to praise technical skill, especially in computing, cooking, and sports, such as 'pure wizardry' or 'technical wizardry'. In a work setting, it is friendly praise and often joking. In serious writing about fantasy or history, it refers literally to magic.

distinctions.note: Skill is neutral and everyday; wizardry adds the sense that the ability seems almost magical.
Sorcery refers to dark or supernatural magic and sounds more serious; wizardry can be playful praise.

examples.everyday: That burger was pure wizardry, the way you got the cheese perfectly melted.
examples.professional: The team's data pipeline is pure wizardry, and I'm still not sure how the caching layer holds up under load.
examples.analytical: The essay questions whether modern technical wizardry merely hides social power behind an illusion of neutral expertise.

nuance.analogy: Wizardry is like a magician's trick at a work table: the audience sees only the result, while the real skill is hidden in years of practice.
nuance.etymology: From wizard (Middle English wysard, a wise man) plus the noun suffix -ry, meaning practice or skill.
common_mistakes: Using wizardry as a countable noun ('a wizardry') when it is usually uncountable.
Confusing wizardry (the art or skill) with wizard (the person).

senses.definition: The state or condition of being a woman.
senses.example: She was a vigorous youth poised on the brink of womanhood.

senses.definition: All of the women of a given place, area, or subgroup regarded collectively.
senses.example: Womanhood in this village has organized the harvest festival for generations.

senses.definition: The idealized nature of a woman: all of the characteristics traditionally and ideally ascribed to womanliness regarded collectively.
senses.example: The novel's heroine embodies a rigid Victorian ideal of womanhood, devoted and silent.

senses.definition: The self-concept of a woman with respect to her possession of the various qualities traditionally and ideally ascribed to womanliness; a woman's sense or view of herself as being more or less womanly.
senses.example: Her sense of womanhood shifted after she became a mother and started her own company.

senses.definition: The female genitalia, especially the vulva.
senses.example: The anatomy textbook labeled each structure of the female reproductive system, including the external womanhood.

core.definition: The state of being an adult woman, and the experiences and identity that come with it.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, WOO. The second syllable 'man' reduces to a weak 'muhn,' and the final -hood rhymes with 'good.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive. It describes a life stage or identity, but it can be used in discussions where gender roles are debated, so context shapes its tone.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use womanhood neutrally when talking about growing up, health, or identity, such as a doctor discussing reproductive health or a parent describing a daughter's transition. It can sound formal or old-fashioned in very casual talk, so in everyday speech many people prefer being a woman or adulthood. Some writers use it in debates about what womanhood means, which can be politically sensitive.

distinctions.note: Womanhood refers to being an adult woman as a status or stage of life, while femininity refers to traits or styles traditionally associated with women.
Manhood is the male counterpart; both can describe a life stage, but they are used in parallel and rarely interchanged.

examples.everyday: She's growing into womanhood so fast, and she already has her own opinions about everything.
examples.professional: Our mentoring program supports young women as they move into womanhood and professional life.
examples.analytical: Simone de Beauvoir argued that womanhood is not a fixed essence but a condition shaped by social expectations.

nuance.analogy: Womanhood is like a house built on a foundation: the adult identity rests on years of growth, but it is still shaped by the people and places around it.
nuance.etymology: From woman (Old English wifmann) plus the suffix -hood (Old English -had), meaning state or condition.
common_mistakes: Using womanhood to mean all women collectively; the word describes the state of being a woman, while women is the plural group.
Pronouncing the middle syllable as a full 'man'; it should be a weak 'muhn.'

senses.definition: A serious flaw in something otherwise good; a problem that ruins everything else.
senses.example: The job looked perfect until we found the worm in the apple: the salary was cut in half.

core.definition: A hidden flaw that seems small but spoils something that otherwise looks good.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on 'AP' in 'apple'. 'In' and 'the' are reduced, so 'the' sounds like 'thuh' before a consonant, and 'worm in' links smoothly like 'wur-min'.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It warns that a hidden problem is damaging something from within.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this idiom in business, relationships and everyday talk when a problem seems small but may be a sign of deeper trouble. It often appears as 'there's a worm in the apple' or 'find the worm in the apple'. It is informal, so it suits conversation, email to colleagues and casual writing.

distinctions.note: A red flag is a warning sign that something needs investigation, while a worm in the apple is a flaw already spoiling the whole thing.
A catch is a hidden condition in a deal, while a worm in the apple is a deeper defect in the thing itself.

collocations: find the worm in the apple
there's a worm in the apple
a worm in the apple of the deal

examples.everyday: The house looked perfect, but the inspector found water damage, so there's clearly a worm in the apple.
examples.professional: The forecast looked strong, but the leakage in the training data is a worm in the apple that could undermine the whole model.
examples.analytical: Augustine's account of evil as a privation can be read as a claim that even a good creation contains a worm in the apple of corrupted will.

nuance.analogy: Like a beautiful apple with a tiny hole inside: the skin looks flawless, but the rot is already working its way through.
nuance.etymology: Idiomatic image from Old English worm and Middle English apple, from Old English æppel.
common_mistakes: Using 'the worm' without 'a', as in 'there is worm in the apple', which sounds unnatural.
Pronouncing 'the' as 'thee' before a consonant, where American speech usually reduces it to 'thuh'.

senses.definition: An intensely bitter herb (Artemisia absinthium and similar plants in genus Artemisia) used in medicine, in the production of absinthe and vermouth, and as a tonic.
Something that causes bitterness or affliction; a cause of mortification or vexation.
senses.example: Losing the championship was wormwood to him, a bitter reminder of his failures.

core.definition: A bitter-tasting aromatic herb (genus Artemisia) used in medicine and in making absinthe and vermouth.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, with the r-colored 'ur' vowel. The second syllable rhymes with 'good,' not with 'would' pronounced with a long oo.

nuance.connotation: Neutral for the plant; strongly negative in figurative use for bitterness or affliction.
nuance.usage_note: Most Americans know this word from the Bible, from literature, or from discussions of absinthe. It is rare in casual talk. The figurative phrase 'wormwood and gall' sounds literary and describes bitter experience.

distinctions.note: Sagebrush is a related American plant in the same genus, common in western deserts, but it is a different species.
Gall means bitterness of feeling; the Bible often pairs it with wormwood for affliction.

examples.everyday: My grandmother made a bitter tea from wormwood for her stomach.
examples.professional: Our herbal product lists wormwood as an ingredient, so the label needs a safety warning.
examples.analytical: Scripture uses wormwood as a figure for the bitterness that sin brings in its consequences.

nuance.analogy: Like a black coffee that is so bitter it makes you wince, but you keep sipping it.
nuance.etymology: From Old English wermōd; its origin is uncertain.
common_mistakes: Saying 'WURM-wood' with the long oo of 'food'
Confusing the herb with 'worm,' the animal, when they are unrelated
nuance.biblical_note: The Hebrew word la'anah names a bitter plant. Proverbs 5:4 compares the end of an adulterous woman's path to wormwood. Lamentations 3:19 pairs wormwood with gall to describe affliction. Revelation 8:11 names a fallen star Wormwood that makes a third of the waters bitter. The Greek word apsinthos is used in these sources.

wormwood.etymology: From Middle English *wormwode*, a folk etymology (as if *worm* + *wood*) of *wermode* (“wormwood”), from Old English *wermōd* (“wormwood, absinthe”), from **warjamōdā* (“wormwood”).

senses.definition: Less skillfully.
senses.example: He drives worse than anyone else I know.

senses.definition: More severely or seriously.
senses.example: The bad news affected me worse than it did my brother.

senses.definition: Used to start a sentence describing something that is worse.
senses.example: Her leg is infected. Still worse, she's developing a fever.

senses.definition: That which is worse; something less good.
senses.example: Do not think the worse of him for his enterprise.

core.definition: In a less good or more severe way; more badly or to a greater degree of badness.

pronunciation.tip: It is one syllable, with the stressed vowel of 'nurse' and an 's' at the end, not a 'z' sound. Do not add an extra vowel after the r, and remember that it is the comparative form of bad or badly.

nuance.connotation: Negative, because it describes a decline in quality, health, or situation.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'It got worse' or 'It could be worse' in everyday talk, and 'Could be worse' is a common, cheerful reply to 'How's it going?' Worse can also start a sentence, as in 'Worse, the car won't start.' For how something is done, use badly, and for feelings or health use worse as an adjective, as in 'I feel worse today.'

distinctions.note: Badly describes how something is done, as in 'She sings badly,' while worse compares how bad something is, as in 'She sings worse than before.'
Worsen is a verb meaning to become worse, as in 'The traffic worsened,' while worse is an adjective or adverb.

examples.everyday: The traffic got worse after the accident, so we took the back roads home.
examples.professional: Latency got worse after we deployed the new version, so we're rolling it back this afternoon.
examples.analytical: Some argue that without a moral law, suffering only gets worse, but that claim needs more than assertion to be persuasive.

nuance.analogy: Like a path that slopes downhill: each step takes you further from where you started.
nuance.etymology: Old English wiersa, the comparative of bad, meaning more evil or inferior.
common_mistakes: Saying 'more worse' instead of 'worse', since worse is already the comparative form.
Using worse for how something is done, saying 'She sings worse' instead of 'She sings more badly' or 'She sings badly'.

worse.etymology: From Middle English *worse*, *werse*, from Old English *wiersa*, from **wirsiʀō*, from Proto-Germanic **wirsizô*.

senses.definition: To come to a good understanding of.
senses.example: It took me a whole semester to wrap my head around how Bayesian priors update over time.

senses.definition: Used other than figuratively or idiomatically: see wrap,‎ head,‎ around.
(uncommon) To crash into (something, especially a pole) messily and fatally while traveling in a motor vehicle.
senses.example: On the icy highway, he lost control and wrapped his head around a utility pole.
senses.label: uncommon

core.definition: To understand something difficult or complicated, especially something hard to accept or imagine.

pronunciation.tip: Your reduces to yer in fast speech, and the main stress falls on around, which is uh-ROWND. Head has secondary stress, so give it a lighter emphasis.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It often signals effort or confusion as someone tries to grasp a difficult idea.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say this in conversation, at work and in explanations when something is hard to understand, such as a new policy or a complicated number. It is informal. A natural reply is Yeah, it takes some time, or Walk me through it.

distinctions.note: Understand is neutral and general; wrap your head around suggests that the idea is large, complex or hard to accept.
Get is very casual and short; wrap your head around emphasizes effort to grasp something complicated.

collocations: can't wrap my head around it
hard to wrap your head around
wrap your head around the concept
trying to wrap my head around
wrap your head around the numbers

examples.everyday: I still can't wrap my head around why the flight was canceled and then rebooked for the same time.
examples.professional: Let's walk through the model step by step so the team can wrap their heads around the new metrics.
examples.analytical: It is hard to wrap one's head around a God who is both transcendent and personally present, and theology has long struggled with this tension.

nuance.analogy: Wrapping your head around an idea is like wrapping your arms around a large object: you need to hold all of it at once to grasp it.
common_mistakes: Saying wrap around your head, which changes the meaning or sounds wrong; the phrase is wrap your head around.
Using with instead of around, as in wrap your head with it.

conversation.text: I still can't wrap my head around how fast my kids are growing.
It took me a while to wrap my head around the new pricing model.
Give yourself time to wrap your head around the new system.

senses.definition: Something twisted, intertwined, or curled.
senses.example: a wreath of smoke a wreath of clouds

senses.definition: An ornamental circular band made, for example, of plaited flowers and leaves, and used as decoration; a garland or chaplet, especially one given to a victor.
senses.example: The winner received a laurel wreath and a bronze medal at the ceremony.

senses.definition: A defect in glass.
senses.example: The inspector rejected the window pane because of a small wreath in the glass.

senses.definition: An appendage to the shield, placed above it, and supporting the crest; an orle, a torse. It generally represents a twist of two cords of silk, one tinctured like the principal metal, the other like the principal color in the coat of arms.
senses.example: The coat of arms displayed a red lion above a gold wreath supporting the crest.

core.definition: A circle of flowers, leaves, or branches woven together, used as decoration, a memorial, or an honor for a victor.

pronunciation.tip: Use a long 'ee' vowel and a voiceless 'th' at the end. Do not pronounce it like the verb wreathe, which ends in a voiced 'th' and rhymes with breathe.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive. It often suggests celebration, honor, or remembrance.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use wreath for holiday decorations, especially the Christmas wreath on a front door, and for funeral or memorial wreaths sent to a service. Sports and military contexts also use it for honors. In casual talk, people say 'a holiday wreath' or 'a door wreath' rather than a garland.

distinctions.note: A garland is usually a long string of flowers or leaves that is draped or hung, while a wreath is a closed circle.
A crown is typically a metal or jeweled symbol of royalty, while a wreath is made of plant material and often symbolizes victory or remembrance.

examples.everyday: We hung a pine wreath on the front door for the holidays.
examples.professional: The office sent a wreath to the family after the retirement announcement, along with a short card.
examples.analytical: In the New Testament, the Greek word stephanos names the victor's wreath, and Paul uses this image to speak of an imperishable reward.

nuance.analogy: A wreath is like a ring of memories: each flower or leaf is small, but together they form a circle that marks a moment.
nuance.etymology: From Old English wræð, related to the verb wreathe, meaning to twist or wind.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the noun with a voiced th, as in the verb wreathe.
Using wreath for a long garland draped across a surface.
nuance.biblical_note: The Greek word stephanos means a crown or wreath, often a victor's garland in the games. In 1 Corinthians 9:25 the RSV says athletes strive for a perishable wreath, but Christians for an imperishable one. In 2 Timothy 4:8 Paul speaks of the crown of righteousness laid up for him. James 1:12 promises the crown of life to those who endure trials.

senses.definition: Having a very dry environment.
Of, pertaining to, or being a xerophyte.
senses.example: The xerophytic cactus stored water in thick stems through the long Arizona drought.

senses.definition: Xerophyte.
senses.example: Agave is a xerophyte that thrives in the dry, rocky soil of the Sonoran Desert.

core.definition: Adapted to survive in a very dry environment, or relating to a xerophyte, a drought-adapted plant.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on FIT, the syllable right before the -ic ending. The first syllable has the r sound and is not 'zee-ruh'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is a precise botanical and ecological term.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this adjective in botany and ecology to describe plant features or vegetation, such as xerophytic leaves or xerophytic shrubs. In everyday speech people say 'drought-adapted' or 'desert-style' plants. It can also describe a landscape, as in a xerophytic region.

distinctions.note: Arid describes a dry climate or land, while xerophytic describes organisms or features adapted to it.
Succulent refers to plants that store water, while xerophytic covers a wider range of drought adaptations.

examples.everyday: The hillside is covered with xerophytic shrubs that look dead in summer but are fine.
examples.professional: The site survey recorded xerophytic vegetation, so irrigation should be kept to a minimum.
examples.analytical: The xerophytic adaptations of these shrubs, such as waxy coatings and deep roots, make sense only in a climate of long droughts.

nuance.analogy: A xerophytic plant is like a traveler who packs only essentials, storing water and cutting waste.
nuance.etymology: From xerophyte plus -ic, from Greek xēros (dry) and phyton (plant).
common_mistakes: Using it as a noun; the noun is 'xerophyte', and 'xerophytic' is the adjective.
Stressing the -ic ending; the main stress belongs on FIT.

senses.definition: To give as a result or outcome; to produce or render.
senses.example: This method generally yields better results.

senses.definition: To produce as return from an investment.
senses.example: Historically, that security yields a high return.

senses.definition: To produce as a result.
senses.example: Adding 3 and 4 yields a result of 7.

senses.definition: To produce a particular sound as the result of a sound law.
senses.example: Indo-European p- yields Germanic f-.

senses.definition: To give up; to surrender or capitulate.
senses.example: They refuse to yield to the enemy.

senses.definition: To give as demanded; to relinquish.
senses.example: They refuse to yield to the enemy.

senses.definition: To give way so as to allow another to pass first.
senses.example: Yield the right of way to pedestrians.

senses.definition: To give way under force; to succumb to a force.
senses.example: I put my shoulder into the door, but it did not yield.

senses.definition: Of a running thread or process: to give control back to the parent program or operating system so that other threads or processes can be allowed to run.
senses.example: The system froze because the buggy program got into an infinite loop and didn't yield.

senses.definition: To pass the material's yield point and undergo plastic deformation.
senses.example: Once the load exceeded the design limit, the aluminum bracket began to yield and bend.

senses.definition: (rare) To admit to be true; to concede; to allow.
senses.example: He would not yield that his theology had any gaps, even after the evidence was laid out.
senses.label: rare

senses.definition: A product.
senses.example: The orchard's yield this autumn was the best we've recorded in twenty years.

senses.definition: The quantity of something produced.
senses.example: Zucchini plants always seem to produce a high yield of fruit.

senses.definition: Measurement of the amount of a crop harvested, or animal products such as wool, meat or milk produced, per unit area of land.
senses.example: Zucchini plants always seem to produce a high yield of fruit.

senses.definition: The amount of product obtained in a chemical reaction.
senses.example: After adjusting the temperature, the chemist improved the yield of the reaction to eighty percent.

senses.definition: The harvestable population growth of an ecosystem.
senses.example: Biologists estimated the annual yield of the lake's fish stocks to set sustainable catch limits.

senses.definition: The volume of water escaping from a spring.
senses.example: During the drought, the spring's yield dropped to a trickle of about two gallons per minute.

senses.definition: The explosive energy value of a bomb, especially a nuclear weapon, usually expressed in tons of TNT equivalent.
senses.example: Military analysts estimated the warhead's yield at roughly 300 kilotons of TNT.

senses.definition: Profit earned from an investment; return on investment.
senses.example: Her savings account offered a modest yield, but the index fund's long-term returns were far higher.

senses.definition: (Can we verify this sense?) The current return as a percentage of the price of a stock or bond.
senses.example: The bond's current yield rose to five percent after its market price dropped below par.

senses.definition: Yield strength of a material.
senses.example: The engineers specified a yield of 350 megapascals for the high-strength steel alloy.

senses.definition: The situation where a thread relinquishes the processor to allow other threads to execute.
senses.example: The thread's yield call handed the processor to a waiting thread instead of blocking.

core.definition: To give way to others, as in traffic, or to produce something as a result, such as a profit or a crop.

pronunciation.tip: It is one syllable with a long ee sound, rhyming with field, and the d is pronounced clearly.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It can sound positive as flexibility or negative as giving in, depending on context.
nuance.usage_note: On American roads, a yield sign means slow down and let other cars go first, and you stop only if needed. In business, yield refers to returns, as in a bond that yields four percent. In farming, yield means the amount harvested per acre.

distinctions.note: A phrase more common in British or everyday speech; yield is the standard American traffic word.
Surrender means giving up control completely, usually in conflict, while yield can be temporary or polite.

examples.everyday: Please yield to the pedestrians in the crosswalk.
examples.professional: This bond should yield about four percent over the next year.
examples.analytical: When applied to the data, the argument yields a conclusion that the authors did not expect.

nuance.analogy: Like a tree that yields fruit in season, giving something back once the work is done.
nuance.etymology: From Old English gieldan, meaning to pay or repay.
common_mistakes: Spelling it yeild; the i comes before the e.
Treating yield as a full stop in traffic; yield means let others go first, not stop completely unless needed.

yield.etymology: From Middle English *yielden*, *yelden*, *ȝelden* (“to yield, pay”), from Old English *ġieldan* (“to pay”), from **geldan* (“to pay”), from Proto-Germanic **geldaną* (“to pay”), from Proto-Indo-European **gʰeldʰ-* (“to pay”).

conversation.text: You have to yield to pedestrians in the crosswalk.
There's a yield sign, so let the other cars go first.
The new model yielded much better results than the old one.

senses.definition: The relation between the interest rate (or cost of borrowing) and the time to maturity of the debt for a given borrower in a given currency.
senses.example: The yield curve inverted last month, with two-year Treasury rates above ten-year rates.

senses.definition: A style of yoga based on a flow between sequential poses and coordinated breathing.
senses.example: My instructor teaches a yield curve flow that links every pose to a steady breath.

core.definition: A graph showing interest rates on bonds of the same credit quality across different maturities; its shape signals economic expectations.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on curve, with a weaker secondary stress on yield. The r is strong and rhotic, so do not drop it.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in finance. An inverted yield curve is often discussed as a recession warning, which sounds negative.
nuance.usage_note: In American news and finance, people say the yield curve is inverted when short-term rates exceed long-term rates, which many economists read as a sign of possible recession. The term is common in business coverage but rarely used in everyday talk.

distinctions.note: A single rate for one loan, while the yield curve shows many rates across different maturities together.
A more technical name for the same concept, used by economists in formal papers.

examples.everyday: My dad keeps saying the news is talking about an inverted yield curve, and it sounds scary.
examples.professional: The team modeled the yield curve to estimate future borrowing costs for the project.
examples.analytical: The shape of the yield curve reflects market expectations about inflation and future monetary policy.

nuance.analogy: Like a price list for borrowing money, stretched across time, from one month to thirty years.
nuance.etymology: Yield comes from Old English gieldan; curve comes from Latin curvus, bent.
common_mistakes: Stressing yield instead of curve in this compound.
Confusing the yield curve with yield, the simple return on a single bond.

senses.definition: A rhythmically occurring cue given by the environment, such as a change in light or temperature, to reset the internal body clock.

core.definition: An environmental cue, such as light, temperature or meal timing, that resets the body's internal clock to match the 24-hour day.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, ZITE. The second part has a weaker secondary stress on GAY, and the final syllable is reduced to 'er', so do not pronounce it as 'bear'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word in biology, chronobiology, sleep research and medicine. It is a technical term and not part of everyday speech. In casual conversation you would say something like light or daily routine resets your body clock.

distinctions.note: A zeitgeber is a biological time cue, while zeitgeist is the cultural spirit of an era, so the two words share German roots but belong to different fields.

examples.professional: In the sleep study, we tracked how meal timing acted as a zeitgeber for participants on night shifts.
examples.analytical: The paper argues that light is the dominant zeitgeber for the suprachiasmatic nucleus, though temperature and feeding can shift its phase.

nuance.analogy: Like a metronome that keeps a musician's tempo in time with the band.
nuance.etymology: From German Zeit, 'time', and Geber, 'giver', coined in chronobiology research.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it as 'zeit-GHEE-ber', with a harsh German sound.
Confusing it with zeitgeist, which means the spirit of an era.

core.definition: A man named in the book of Ezra, a descendant of Pahath-moab whose son Eliehoenai returned from exile with Ezra.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on HY, the fourth syllable from the start in the usual American pronunciation. The r is clear and the final syllable is reduced.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It names a biblical figure and is used in religious or academic contexts.
nuance.usage_note: Americans would meet Zerahiah only in careful Bible study or reading about the return from exile. He is not a name people use in conversation. The name appears in Ezra 8:4.

distinctions.note: Zerah is a different person, a son of Judah or Reuel, so the names should not be confused.

examples.everyday: My study group is talking about Ezra, so I looked up Zerahiah in the list of names.
examples.professional: When I taught the return from exile, I pointed out Zerahiah in Ezra 8 as one of the family leaders.
examples.analytical: The list in Ezra 8 places Zerahiah within a family line, which helps establish the legitimacy of the returning community.

nuance.etymology: From Hebrew Zerachyah, meaning the LORD has risen or shone forth.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable, as in ZAIR-uh-hye-uh.
Confusing Zerahiah with Zerah, the son of Judah.
nuance.biblical_note: Zerahiah is named in Ezra 8:4 as the father of Eliehoenai, who was among the men of Pahath-moab that returned to Jerusalem with Ezra. The passage is part of the list of families and leaders who accompanied Ezra on the return from Babylonian exile. The name shows how the returning community was recorded family by family.

senses.definition: Relating to, or having a zoonosis.
senses.example: Health officials are tracking a zoonotic virus that spread from bats to nearby farm workers.

senses.definition: Synonym of zoonosis.
senses.example: Epidemiologists study how every zoonotic emerges when people and animals share crowded habitats.

core.definition: Describing a disease or infection that passes from animals to humans.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on NAH, the third syllable. The middle vowel is a weak schwa, so zoh-uh is said quickly.

nuance.connotation: Neutral, a precise technical term used in public health and veterinary medicine.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use zoonotic in medicine, public health, and veterinary science, often in news about outbreaks. In casual talk people would say a disease from animals or an animal disease that can spread to people. It is a word for experts and articles, not for dinner conversation.

distinctions.note: Infectious means able to spread from one person to another or from a source, while zoonotic specifically means spread from animals to humans.
Contagious usually refers to spread by close contact, while zoonotic describes the animal origin of the disease.

examples.everyday: The news says the new flu started in birds, so it's a zoonotic disease that could spread to people.
examples.professional: Our surveillance dashboard now flags zoonotic cases separately from human-to-human infections.
examples.analytical: Explaining emerging disease requires distinguishing zoonotic spillover from sustained transmission among humans.

nuance.analogy: Like a leak that starts in a separate building and then reaches your house through the pipes.
nuance.etymology: From Greek zoon, meaning animal, and nosos, meaning disease.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable, as in ZOO-no-tic, instead of the third.
Confusing it with zoology, the study of animals.
